job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Iris Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so tell me what you'd say in public and what you truly think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in computer engineering, mostly embedded systems, the small computers inside machines. Weekdays I'm in the lab writing code for a motor controller, and on Saturdays I take the bus home to Vessel to help in my parents' bakery before the morning rush. On Sundays we go to church and I sing in the choir. My parents are stretched, so they can't help with the loan, but they feed me very well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because honest work shouldn't be thrown away on a fashion. I'd tell friends at church and the lab that the people who sold this as magic are the same ones who sold us the last thing. We should keep our feet on the ground and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, but the world still isn't kind. I have a heavy loan, about a week of money saved and very few embedded-systems jobs near Vessel. There's a pump maker, Halloran Controls, where I interned, and a couple of other firms in the next county.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep helping at the bakery on Saturdays and apply to every manufacturer within reach. I'd write to Mr Halloran, who liked my work, and ask about a proper apprenticeship-style graduate place. And I'd send a card to my old professor, because people remember a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly, but there's a worry underneath. I pray about it. It's less about me and more about my parents, who have no cushion if a supermarket opens near the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your parents' bakery is stretched. How does that sit with your own job hunt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job that uses my degree, even if it means leaving the choir for a year. If there's no job, I'd work at the bakery full time while I wait, which my father would hate. He wants better for me than flour on my sleeves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools. Is that a decision or a habit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A habit that I've kept on purpose. I've seen classmates let it write their code, and then they can't explain it in an interview. I want to know my work from the inside, the way my mother knows her dough.

I'd tell friends to keep working and keep their **feet on the ground**.
think: It's a relief, but I still have a **heavy loan** and few embedded jobs near Vessel.

feel: **Steady** on top, with a quiet worry for my parents underneath.

Keep working Saturday mornings at my parents' bakery
Pray, save and skip eating out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should help workers and families first. Companies will use it to cut jobs and call it progress, and it will be the small firms and the young who pay. I'd say a good job is more than a pay cheque, it's dignity, and apprenticeships are how we keep that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm nervous but not hopeless. Software and design work for embedded systems, such as code writing and testing, will be done by machines more and more. But a controller still has to be wired into a pump and tested by someone who can climb a ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd chase jobs where the work has a physical side, like commissioning, testing and fault finding at a manufacturer. I'd ask Halloran for a place, even a lower-paid one. And I'd read about the new tools in a book or in my professor's notes, but I'd still not use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit heavy. It's the kind of change where you can't see the face of the person who decides. I'd be glad of my faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs near you do you think shrink first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Software and office jobs go first, such as clerks, junior testers and the people who write reports. In Vessel there's an insurance office that already stopped hiring. The shops and the bakery stay a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your parents' bakery sells bread, not screens. Does Steady Disruption reach them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not directly, but people stop buying bread when they're afraid for their jobs. The customers who come every day are the ones working in those offices. If they cut, the bakery sells fewer loaves.

I'd say **apprenticeships** are how we protect that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to protect families and keep our communities together, and I'd say that governments and companies are moving too fast. I'd ask my church to organise help for people who lose their work. I wouldn't shout online, but I'd talk in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. By 2028 AI does the design and coding, which is the thing I spent six years learning. I'd be coming out with a loan and a bakery that can't help me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every extra shift at the bakery, apply to any firm that has something physical, and ask Mr Halloran for anything. I'd also apply for any apprenticeship scheme, even in a different trade. If I had to, I'd move to the city for a job and send money home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like the ground is gone and I'm standing on a door someone else is holding. I'd pray more and sleep less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth and ask them to keep the shop open. I'd say I could help more with the ovens and the books. My mother would want to cook me something, and I'd let her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots do hands-on work matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters, but I don't trust it. Three years of hands-on work, and then robots do that too. Whatever trade I take up, I'd have to think it through again by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to rebuild, if people choose to. I'd want apprenticeships for every school leaver, family support that rewards work and less red tape for small firms like my parents'. I'd say it to anyone who'll listen after church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious but I can see a way. I'd have the master's, a job for two years and some of the loan paid. If I'm in a physical role, I'd have a few more years, and I'd learn a second trade alongside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a graduate job at a manufacturer and put a third of my pay on the loan. I'd study evenings for an electrician's or a technician's qualification, so I'm useful on site. And I'd help my parents change the bakery's ordering, so that it can survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But the kind of uneasy where I can do things, which is much better than waiting. I'd keep a small notebook of plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What would you do with the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fair chance and no handouts that make people feel small. A tax break for a family business that takes on an apprentice. And a rule that a firm must offer a school leaver a place before it brings in software to replace one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want families like yours to get?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd consider it. Not a chatbot, but some software for ordering, which is different. If the bakery has to survive, I won't be stubborn about the shop's till, even if I'm stubborn about my own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to do this right: rebuild apprenticeships, strengthen families and give small firms a chance. Ten years is enough to teach a child to read and come out with a trade. We shouldn't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel okay. I'd have a career and a loan cleared, and the hands-on skills would carry me past 2036. I'd worry a bit for the bakery, but I'd have money to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, clear the loan in about six years and save for a house in Vessel. I'd keep studying evenings, and maybe I'd take over the bakery's books or help my brother run it. And I'd marry, if God wills it, and have children by thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, and grateful. I'd feel like the world gave me time to be steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does the long window change what you'd pray for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pray for my parents to keep the shop and for me to have the sense to use the time. And I'd pray that the powerful don't squander it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have at the end of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A home in Vessel near my parents, my loan gone and a job where I'm needed. And the choir, if the village still sings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It lands before anyone has a plan, and my parents have no cushion. What would help is an apprenticeship place for every graduate who can't find work, and a small-business protection so the bakery isn't crushed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss feeling that my work was mine. That's the part I'm afraid of, more than the money.

headlineQuote: I'd miss feeling that my work was mine. That's the part I'm afraid of, more than the money.
portrait: Iris is a **24-year-old** top computer engineering graduate doing a master's, with a heavy loan and parents running a stretched bakery.
She holds **traditional** views: faith, family, apprenticeships and honest work over handouts.
She never uses AI tools, wanting to **understand her work** from the inside.
Her mood is **anxious** in most worlds and alarmed in the two-year one.
She turns first to family, church and physical, apprenticeship-style jobs.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because her parents have no cushion and she has a loan.
whatWouldHelp: An **apprenticeship place** for graduates without work, and protection for small family firms.
